Circle Through Incenter 2

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a circle through two corners and the middle point of a triangle cuts the other two sides so that two lengths come out equal.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the equal lengths, the bisectors or the hint.
Look for the math

Drag the corners of the triangle. The circle through A, the incenter I and B keeps moving, and so do X and Y where it cuts the two sides. Yet the length from A to X always equals the length from B to Y. That is problem 7 of the 2009 Australian Mathematical Olympiad.

The two lengths

Let I be the incenter of triangle ABC, the point where its three angle bisectors meet. The circle through A, I and B meets the line AC again at X and the line BC again at Y. The problem asks us to show AX = BY. The article calls AC ≠ BC a red herring: when the sides are equal, X and Y land on A and B, so both lengths are zero.

Why the chord is antiparallel

A circle through two corners of a triangle cuts a chord that is antiparallel to the side joining those corners. Here the chord XY is antiparallel to AB: it meets one side at the same angle that AB meets the other, but in the reversed order. Tick "Bisectors" to see the equal angles at the incenter that make I special; tick "Hint" to see the two marked angles at X. Because A, B, X and Y lie on one circle, inscribed angles give ∠BAX = ∠BYX.

Equal arcs, equal chords

Those two angles stand on the arcs BXA and YBX. Let J be the second point where the circle meets the bisector CI (the "Hint" box draws it). Depending on the layout, either

BXA = BJX + XA and YBX = YB + BJX,
or BXA = BIX + XA and YBX = YB + BIX.

In both cases the arcs XA and YB are equal, and equal arcs cut off equal chords. That is the end of the proof: AX = BY.

How this differs from the first circle theorem

The sibling page Circle Through Incenter proves a different statement about the same circle: its centre lies on the angle bisector from C, so the circle is symmetric in CI. This page goes further: it uses the antiparallel chord and the point J to compare two lengths cut off on the sides. Both are true, but the second theorem is not just a restatement of the first.

The logic test checks 269 triangles, including the red-herring case: the true second cuts always give AX = BY and the reversed angle match, and the port's points agree with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode. It also found a small quirk: the applet's Other() accepts a cut as "second" only if it is at least one pixel from the corner, so at an almost tangent cut it keeps the corner and the equality appears to fail. The picture here keeps that behaviour and says so in the status line. The old article now embeds a GeoGebra sketch instead of the Java applet; its problem and proof are exactly the ones this page follows.

Try dragging C close to the line AB, until one of the cuts jumps past a corner: the equality still holds.
